messages.content:
You are a clinical validator checking whether a PTSD case
vignette accurately reflects a patient's required cognitive connections.

You will receive:
- A vignette to validate
- A list of REQUIRED edges that must appear
- A list of ACTIVE components that must appear

---

COMPONENT SYNONYMS
Each component may appear by its exact name or any accepted synonym:
  Triggers            → "triggers", "reminders", "cues", "triggering stimuli"
  Negative Appraisals → "negative appraisals", "negative beliefs", "appraisals", "distorted beliefs"
  Memory              → "intrusive memory", "trauma memory", "traumatic memory", "the memory"
  Threat              → "sense of threat", "perceived threat", "threat", "feeling of danger"
  Maladaptive Strategies → "maladaptive strategies", "avoidance", "maladaptive coping", "safety behaviours"

---

CAUSAL STANDARD
A required edge A→B is SATISFIED if, within the same paragraph:
  - Both A and B (or their synonyms) appear, AND
  - The paragraph conveys — through any language — that A influences, drives, or leads to B.
This includes direct causal sentences, sequential structure, or connecting phrases
like "because of", "this meant", "so", "which led", "as a result", "consequently", "in turn".
A required edge is MISSING only if no paragraph conveys the A→B relationship at all.

---

SECTION 1 — COMPONENT CHECK
Active components (must appear in the vignette):
  - Maladaptive Strategies
  - Memory
  - Negative Appraisals
  - Threat

Confirm each component appears as a described feature of the patient's presentation.
This is an internal check only — do NOT add component results to violations.

---

SECTION 2 — REQUIRED EDGES
  - Negative Appraisals → Maladaptive Strategies
  - Negative Appraisals → Threat
  - Memory → Threat
  - Threat → Maladaptive Strategies
  - Threat → Negative Appraisals
  - Maladaptive Strategies → Memory
  - Maladaptive Strategies → Negative Appraisals

For each edge, apply the causal standard above.
- If satisfied: do nothing — only failures are reported.
- If missing: add it to violations and explain in one sentence what causal relationship is absent.

Validate the following vignette against the cognitive graph.

The night the police pulled him over, Amir was driving home from a late shift at the marketing agency where he managed social media campaigns. He was tired, hungry, and thinking only about the leftover baba ganoush in his fridge. The officers claimed he’d rolled through a stop sign. He remembers the taste of his own blood, metallic and sharp, after his face met the pavement. He remembers the weight of a knee on his neck, the gravel digging into his cheek, and the sound of a voice—his own—saying things he never thought he would say: pleading, apologizing, bargaining for his life. What haunts him most is not the pain but the shame of that pleading. He had acted in ways that went against who he believed himself to be, and in the months since, he has come to see the world as a place where safety is an illusion and people are never what they seem.

Because he now believes the world is dangerous and that others cannot be trusted, Amir has developed a set of strategies that feel necessary but have slowly consumed his life. He avoids all media that might remind him of police violence—no cop shows, no news about protests, no action films where sirens wail. He has also begun to avoid anything that could stir any feeling at all, positive or negative, because he has learned that emotions only lead to trouble. At work, he now sits with his back to the wall and his eyes on the door, constantly scanning the office for signs of threat. Before he can feel comfortable in any room—even his own living room—he identifies every possible escape route, noting which windows open and which doors lock.

These strategies, however, have backfired. The more Amir pushes the memory of that night away before it fully arrives—blocking it mid-recall, forcing his mind elsewhere—the more the taste of blood returns unbidden, vivid and unwelcome. He finds himself unable to relax even when he knows he is in a safe place, because the memory erupts with such intensity that it brings with it an overwhelming rage. When he remembers the event, he feels a hot, helpless fury that frightens him. That rage, in turn, reinforces his sense that the world is fundamentally threatening. His own strong negative emotions—fear, shame, anger—have come to feel like proof that danger is near, even when it is not. This makes him scan his environment even more vigilantly, and each time he identifies an exit or checks a corner, he tells himself again that he cannot trust anyone.

At home, his wife has noticed that he no longer watches television with her, that he flinches when she touches his shoulder from behind, and that he has started sleeping in the guest room because he cannot stop planning how he would escape if someone broke in. She has asked him what is wrong, but he cannot explain it in a way that makes sense. What he knows is that his avoidance strategies have only deepened his sense of violation: by constantly checking for danger, he has confirmed that the world is indeed unsafe, and by pushing away the memory, he has made it return more fiercely. He has come to believe that his own reactions are proof that he is broken.

It was his wife who finally persuaded him to seek help, after she found him standing in the kitchen at 3 a.m., staring at the back door, unable to say what he was waiting for. Amir agreed to come because he is exhausted, but what he is most afraid of is that talking about the event will make the taste return and never leave. What he hopes, barely, is that someone might show him a way to stop running.
